newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland, February 28.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland, February 28.

text.p: The following are the highlights of stories from the Irish press on Friday.

- The Irish government is backing the construction of a 113 million Irish pound incinerator in county Dublin which would have the capacity to process 490,000 tonnes of waste a year, or half of all the city's domestic refuse.
- Ben Dunne is prepared to hand over all papers and affidavits to the tribunal of inquiry into the payments to politicians by March 12.
- Bank of Ireland and the Bristol and West Building Society have signed the agreement for the proposed transfer of the British building society business to the bank.

- Irish borrowers have been advised that they should now be considering the impact European Monetary Union will have on interest rates, particularly if they are thinking about converting to a fixed rate loan.
- Divorce got off to a disastrous start on Thursday when first applicants had their cases put on hold due to a shortage of trained staff.
- A swimming coach is to go on trial charged with 90 sexual offences against young girls, 21 years after the first offence allegedly took place.
- The Irish National Lottery on Thursday reported the lowest increase in annual sales in its ten-year history and pointed the finger of blame at its multi-million jackpot competitor - the UK Lottery.
- Sinn Fein has been frozen out of the St Patrick's day celebrations at the White House as the Clinton administration shows its anger at the IRA's refusal to call a new cease-fire.
- The Irish pound's overall value slipped on Thursday as it lost some of Wednesday's gains against continental currencies.
- Divorce floodgates opened on Thursday with over 1,000 applications within minutes of the historic ending of Ireland's ban on marriage dissolution.

- The biggest drugs trial in the history of Ireland arising out of the seizure of 47 million pounds worth of cocaine on a boat in Cork harbour ended on Thursday when the Jury returned a verdict of not guilty against the fourth and final member of the crew to walk free.
- Irish prime Minister John Bruton's visit to Northern Ireland today was in danger of becoming a political circus with unionists united outrage over the trip to the Fermanagh lakelands.
- Though there are fears that the strength of the punt against other European currencies could have implications for industry, it is unlikely to interfere with Irish tourism growth.
